title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
section: Warm-up · three questions from last time
text:
Warm-up · three questions from last time
≈ 5 min · shout it out


A bigram language model predicts the next token from how much context?
What is the cosine similarity of [1, 0] and [0, 1]?
An embedding table for 27 tokens, with 8 dimensions per token — how many parameters?

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Warm-up · answers


Exactly one token — the current one. However long the text, the bigram model conditions on the single most recent token and nothing further back.
\dfrac{(1 \times 0) + (0 \times 1)}{1 \times 1} = \dfrac{0}{1} = 0. The vectors are orthogonal — no overlap in direction at all.
27 \times 8 = 216. No bias term to add: an embedding table is a lookup table, not a layer computation.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
The fixed-input problem
Picking up from yesterday
Last time our bigram model remembered exactly one character

Today we want to give it a running memory



A feed-forward network has a fixed input size:

MLP: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d, one d.
CNN: H \times W \times C images.

But text is variable length. “Yes.” has four characters. The entirety of Hamlet has 175,000.

Insufficient workarounds

Pad / truncate to fixed length (wastes capacity)
Bag-of-words / TF-IDF (throws away order entirely)
Sliding window (caps memory at the window size)

We want something that scales with the sequence.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Sequence ≠ independent observations

The matters order words in of a sentence the.
This introduces dependencies:

The keys, which had been sitting on the table next to the mail and the half-empty coffee mug, were still there.

Notice that “were” corresponds to a subject 16 words away

He said he would come. vs He said he would not come.

Single tokens can flip meaning.

Hamilton, the founder of the Federalist Party, …

A co-reference to a named individual several sentences earlier



A good model has to carry information forward as it reads.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Sequences are everywhere
Not just text


CS / industry

Speech recognition — waveform → words.
Music generation — sequences of MIDI events.
Time-series forecasting — stock prices, server load.
DNA / protein sequences — amino-acid order matters.
Streaming / online learning — events as they arrive.


Social science

Conflict event sequences — Hegre et al. forecasting.
Legislative debate transcripts — order of speakers, framing.
Roll-call voting — sequence of votes within a session.
Survey responses over time — panel data with attrition.
Event-history models — time-to-event with covariates.








Tip


The architecture you’ll meet today applies to all of these. If your data has a natural order and prior elements inform later ones, recurrence is a candidate.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
The recurrent unit, mathematically
At each time step t:

\mathbf{h}_t = \tanh\!\left( \mathbf{W}_{hh} \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_{xh} \mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_h \right)


\hat{\mathbf{y}}_t = \mathbf{W}_{hy} \mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{b}_y



\mathbf{W}_{hh}, \mathbf{W}_{xh}, \mathbf{W}_{hy} — shared across all time steps.
\mathbf{h}_t has fixed dimensionality (say, 128 or 256)
The only way information from step 1 reaches step 50 is through this single hidden state (after going through 49 matmuls)








Note


This is the vanilla RNN (Elman, 1990). The whole architecture is three weight matrices and a \tanh. As we’ll see in Part 2, that simplicity is also its problem.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Example forward pass


Setup

Hidden dim 1. W_{hh} = 0.6, W_{xh} = 1.0, b_h = 0.
\sigma = \tanh. Initial h_0 = 0.
Inputs: x_1 = 0.8, x_2 = -0.4.


Time step 1
h_1 = \tanh(0.6 \cdot 0 + 1.0 \cdot 0.8) = \tanh(0.8) \approx 0.664
Time step 2
h_2 = \tanh(0.6 \cdot 0.664 + 1.0 \cdot (-0.4)) = \tanh(-0.0016) \approx -0.0016


Notice
A negative input all but cancelled the carried-forward signal from x_1. The hidden state is only a small bit of memory, and newer inputs will overwrite older ones.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
section: Isn’t one set of weights a limitation?
text:
Isn’t one set of weights a limitation?


The same \mathbf{W}_{xh} processes every input token.

The model learns one way to look at a token.
The model learns one way to combine current input with prior history.
No “position-specific” weights.

This is the same trick as convolutions

We share parameters across positions



Parameter sharing buys us:

Generalisation — what we learn “here” transfers to “there” too
Variable length — no architectural change needed for longer sequences
Fewer parameters — by orders of magnitude vs. an unrolled MLP

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Generation with an RNN


Start with \mathbf{h}_0 = \mathbf{0}.
Feed in a starting token \mathbf{x}_1.
Compute \mathbf{h}_1, then \hat{\mathbf{y}}_1 — predicted next-token logits.
Sample next token from softmax of \hat{\mathbf{y}}_1.
Use it as \mathbf{x}_2. Compute \mathbf{h}_2. Sample \mathbf{x}_3.
Repeat as long as we want.


Generation is just the forward pass, repeated — same machinery as the bigram model, but with the hidden state carrying memory.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Bidirectional RNNs
For non-generative tasks, you can read both directions


For classifying a sentence or tagging each word, the model can read both forward and backward:
\mathbf{h}_t = [\overrightarrow{\mathbf{h}}_t; \overleftarrow{\mathbf{h}}_t]

Forward RNN reads left → right.
Backward RNN reads right → left.
Concatenate the two hidden states at each position.



Why this isn’t always usable.

For generation, you can’t read the future as it hasn’t been produced yet.
Bidirectional RNNs are for labelling, not generating.
Same constraint applies to attention on Day 10: we have to apply a causal mask for generation, but not for classification.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Stacked RNNs
Depth in space
Layer 1’s hidden states form a sequence. So we can feed them to a second RNN:

\mathbf{h}^{(2)}_t = \tanh\!\left( \mathbf{W}^{(2)}_{hh} \mathbf{h}^{(2)}_{t-1} + \mathbf{W}^{(2)}_{xh} \mathbf{h}^{(1)}_t + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}_h \right)

The superscript is the layer. Layer 2’s “input token” at step t is layer 1’s hidden state \mathbf{h}^{(1)}_t.



Two separable kinds of depth:

Depth in time — how many steps the recurrence runs (stems from the data)
Depth in space — how many layers are stacked (adds more parameters)




Parameter cost per extra layer
Each layer has its own \mathbf{W}_{hh}, \mathbf{W}_{xh}, \mathbf{b}_h. With hidden size 128 at both layers, layer 2 adds:

\begin{aligned}
128^2 + 128^2 + 128 &= 16{,}384 + 16{,}384 + 128 \\
&= 32{,}896
\end{aligned}



Two or three layers was the working norm

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Plenary · unroll a tiny RNN
≈ 12 min · in pairs

A tiny RNN
Hidden dim = 1 (so \mathbf{h}_t is a single number).
Weights: W_{hh} = 0.5,\ W_{xh} = 1.0,\ b_h = 0. Initial h_0 = 0. Use \tanh as the activation.
(Treat the network as outputting h_t directly — skip \mathbf{W}_{hy} for this exercise.)
Inputs at three time steps x_1 = 1.0, \ x_2 = -0.5, \ x_3 = 2.0
Compute
h_1, h_2, h_3 by hand.
Reflect
How much of the original x_1 signal is still detectable in h_3?

Six minutes.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Plenary · answers

Step 1 h_1 = \tanh(0.5 \cdot 0 + 1.0 \cdot 1.0) = \tanh(1.0) \approx 0.762.
Step 2 h_2 = \tanh(0.5 \cdot 0.762 + 1.0 \cdot (-0.5)) = \tanh(-0.119) \approx -0.119.
Step 3 h_3 = \tanh(0.5 \cdot (-0.119) + 1.0 \cdot 2.0) = \tanh(1.94) \approx 0.959.


The reflection By step 3, the input x_3 = 2.0 has dominated. The signal from x_1 has been (a) multiplied by 0.5 at step 2, (b) squashed through \tanh at step 2, (c) multiplied by 0.5 at step 3, (d) squashed through \tanh at step 3.
That sequence of multiplications and saturations is the vanishing gradient problem, in miniature.

text:
Teacher forcing
What do we feed in when the model guesses wrong?
Training on the word hello. At each step the model predicts the next character:




Step

At step 3 we feed in the true previous character (“l” from the corpus), not the “x” the model produced. This is called teacher forcing.


Every position has a known target from the corpus
The loss decomposes per step: L = \sum_t L_t — one cross-entropy per position
A wrong guess costs loss at its own step but doesn’t derail the next one

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Generation cannot use a teacher


Training
Inputs always come from the corpus. The model reads true history at every step, mistakes or not.

Generation
The sampled token becomes the next input. The model ingests its own output, so one wrong early token feeds every later prediction


We call this mismatch exposure bias.

The model never sees its own mistakes during training, but has to accept them at generation

The alternative – training on the model’s own samples – means sampling a sequence at every training step. Slow, and in practice unstable.

Transformers train with teacher forcing too, token for token

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Truncated BPTT
Training on texts too long to unroll
You cannot backpropagate through a million-token book:

The graph holds every hidden state in memory, and the gradient product runs over every step.


Truncated BPTT:

Chop the text into windows of, e.g., 128 steps.
Run forward and backward within each window; update the weights.
Carry the final hidden state into the next window as its \mathbf{h}_0.
We detach this hidden state first, to prevent carrying gradients over




Truncation preserves memory
The hidden state flows across the window boundary, so the model can carry context from window to window.

Truncation cuts off gradient
No gradient crosses the boundary, so nothing more than 128 steps back affects the current update.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Vanishing & exploding gradients
The gradient of the loss w.r.t. \mathbf{h}_1:

\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{h}_1} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{h}_T} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_T}{\partial \mathbf{h}_{T-1}} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_2}{\partial \mathbf{h}_1}

Each factor \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_t}{\partial \mathbf{h}_{t-1}} is the matrix of partial derivatives of \mathbf{h}_t with respect to \mathbf{h}_{t-1}.
With T multiplications of similar matrices, and magnitudes generally < 1, the product shrinks.

And if > 1, it explodes.



Vanishing
Early steps stop learning. The model effectively has no long-range memory.
This is the harder problem.

Exploding
Training diverges, but can be fixed in practice with gradient clipping.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Vanilla RNNs struggle past ~50 tokens
Recall \tanh' peaks at 1 and falls off fast. For |z| > 5, \tanh'(z) < 0.001.

After 50 multiplications by a matrix whose largest singular value is, e.g., 0.5:

0.5^{50} \approx 8.9 \times 10^{-16}

About 10^{-15} of the signal arrives.

So whatever happened 50 steps ago has no measurable influence on the update.








Often, real RNNs degrade well before 50 tokens


RNNs handle sequences of 5–20 tokens reasonably well, but any larger and you need some variant.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Activity · find the vanishing gradient
≈ 8 min · in pairs

A vanilla RNN with hidden dim 1, W_{hh} = 0.3, W_{xh} = 1.0, b_h = 0, \tanh activation.
Inputs: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{10} — all equal to 1.0.
Compute (approximately)

h_1, h_2, h_5, h_{10}.
Estimate \dfrac{\partial h_{10}}{\partial h_5} — what’s the magnitude?
Interpretation: if I change x_5 by a small amount, how much does h_{10} change?


Six minutes.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Activity · answer

Trajectory of h_t
h_1 = \tanh(1.0) \approx 0.762. Then each step: h_{t+1} = \tanh(0.3 h_t + 1.0).
Numerically: h_2 = \tanh(1.2285) \approx 0.842, h_3 = \tanh(1.2527) \approx 0.849, …, converges to a fixed point ≈ 0.850.


Gradient
\dfrac{\partial h_{t+1}}{\partial h_t} = (1 - h_{t+1}^2) \cdot 0.3.
At convergence (h \approx 0.850): (1 - 0.850^2)(0.3) = (0.2775)(0.3) \approx 0.083.
So \dfrac{\partial h_{10}}{\partial h_5} \approx 0.083^5 \approx 3.9 \times 10^{-6}.


Interpretation Changing x_5 moves h_{10} by about a millionth of the change you made. The signal vanished in 5 steps.
Backprop can’t tell the network that x_5 matters for predicting \hat{y}_{10}. Training stalls on long-range dependencies.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Exploding gradients
This is the same mechanism but run the other way
If we drop the \tanh (a simplification), the linear RNN:
h_t = 1.5\, h_{t-1} + x_t
has a backward step that now multiplies the gradient by 1.5:

\frac{\partial h_{10}}{\partial h_5} = 1.5^5 \approx 7.6 \qquad\qquad 1.5^{50} \approx 6.4 \times 10^8

Fifty steps turn 1.5 into 640 million!
With the \tanh back in, each factor is W_{hh} \tanh'(\cdot) — messier, but these failure modes remain.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Gradient clipping
For exploding gradients we can be pragmatic


Algorithm: after backprop, compute the norm of all gradients. If it exceeds a threshold (e.g. 1.0 or 5.0), rescale all gradients to that threshold.
torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(
    model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0
)

Can be added to every RNN training loop in practice.
Stops the loss from going NaN as L \to \infty








Doesn’t solve vanishing gradients


To “clip” a number close to 0 would only worsen the problem!




For exploding, clipping is enough.

An example of “if the maths is unstable, just truncate” that recurs across deep learning

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Gated multiplication
Clipping handled exploding. For vanishing, the fix is a multiply the network controls
A gate is a vector with entries between 0 and 1, produced by a small sigmoid layer with its own learned weights:

\mathbf{g} = \sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_g [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_g\right)

[\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] stacks the two vectors into one long input — notation we’ll reuse for the LSTM.
Applying a gate is element-wise multiplication (the Hadamard product), written \odot:

Multiply matching entries of two equal-shaped vectors




Worked example

\begin{bmatrix} 1.0 \\ 0.5 \\ 0.0 \end{bmatrix} \odot \begin{bmatrix} 4.0 \\ -2.0 \\ 5.0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4.0 \\ -1.0 \\ 0.0 \end{bmatrix}

Maintains the same shape.


Why a gate helps
\mathbf{W}_g is learned and \mathbf{g} is recomputed at every step, so the network reads \mathbf{h}_{t-1} and \mathbf{x}_t and decides what passes.

The \tanh chain multiplied by \approx 0.083 per step whether the signal mattered or not. A gate can learn to open fully and multiply by $$1.0.


\sigma never reaches 0 or 1 exactly and instead sits at values like 0.002 or 0.998

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Gated RNNs


LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997)
A cell state \mathbf{c}_t that can carry information across many steps with only gated multiplications

Enabling gradients to survive much longer

Three gates:

Forget: drop bits of \mathbf{c}_{t-1}.
Input: add bits to \mathbf{c}_t.
Output: expose part of \mathbf{c}_t as \mathbf{h}_t.


GRU
A simpler version (Cho et al. 2014)

Fewer gates than LSTM
Comparable performance on most tasks
Cheaper

This is the default RNN variant in many libraries


LSTMs and GRUs were the state of the art for sequence tasks from ~2014 to 2017. Then came transformers — the story at the end of today, and all of Monday.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Inside an LSTM cell
The diagram first — the equations come next slide

Three gates + a cell state

Forget gate \mathbf{f}_t — how much of the previous cell state \mathbf{c}_{t-1} to keep.
Input gate \mathbf{i}_t — how much of the new candidate \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t to write.
Output gate \mathbf{o}_t — how much of the updated \mathbf{c}_t to expose as the hidden state.

The straight path along the top — \mathbf{c}_{t-1} \to \mathbf{c}_t — is the memory highway: information rides it with only a multiply and an add.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
The LSTM, in equations
Same picture, written out. Each gate is its own sigmoid layer; \odot is the element-wise multiply from the gating slide.


\mathbf{f}_t = \sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_f [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_f\right) \mathbf{i}_t = \sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_i [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_i\right) \mathbf{o}_t = \sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_o [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_o\right) \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t = \tanh\!\left(\mathbf{W}_c [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_c\right) \mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t \mathbf{h}_t = \mathbf{o}_t \odot \tanh(\mathbf{c}_t)

The three gates are sigmoids, so each entry sits in [0, 1] — a soft “how much to let through”.

Worked forget-gate number
A forget gate of f_t = 0.9 keeps 90% of the old cell value: if c_{t-1} = 2.0, the forget step alone passes 0.9 \times 2.0 = 1.8 forward. A gate of 0.1 would pass only 0.1 \times 2.0 = 0.2.

The cell update is additive — gradients flow along \mathbf{c} without shrinking.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
One LSTM step by hand
One dimension of everything, so each quantity is a single number


Setup

h_0 = 0, c_0 = 0, input x_1 = 1.
Each weight matrix is a pair [\,\text{weight on } h_{t-1},\ \text{weight on } x_t\,]:


W_f = [0,\ 0.5]
W_i = W_o = W_c = [0,\ 1]
b_f = b_i = b_o = b_c = 0


The three gates
f_1 = \sigma(0 \times 0 + 0.5 \times 1 + 0) = \sigma(0.5) \approx 0.62
i_1 = \sigma(0 \times 0 + 1 \times 1 + 0) = \sigma(1) \approx 0.73
o_1 = \sigma(0 \times 0 + 1 \times 1 + 0) = \sigma(1) \approx 0.73
All three numbers are between 0 and 1.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
section: One LSTM step by hand — memory and output
text:
One LSTM step by hand — memory and output
In one dimension, \odot is just multiplication

Candidate
\tilde{c}_1 = \tanh(0 \times 0 + 1 \times 1 + 0) = \tanh(1) \approx 0.76
Memory update
c_1 = f_1 c_0 + i_1 \tilde{c}_1 \approx (0.62 \times 0) + (0.73 \times 0.76) \approx 0.56
Output
h_1 = o_1 \tanh(c_1) \approx 0.73 \times \tanh(0.56) \approx 0.73 \times 0.51 \approx 0.37

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
section: One LSTM step by hand — reading the numbers
text:
One LSTM step by hand — reading the numbers


f_1 \approx 0.62 — keep 62% of the old memory. (c_0 = 0 here, so there was nothing to keep yet.)
i_1 \approx 0.73 — write 73% of the new candidate into memory.
o_1 \approx 0.73 — expose 73% of the (squashed) memory as the hidden state.


Each gate is a learned dial between 0 and 1.

In a trained model the forget gate might sit near 1 while a name is being spelled out…
… then drop towards 0 at a full stop

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
section: Inside a GRU cell — the simpler cousin
text:
Inside a GRU cell — the simpler cousin
Cho et al. (2014) — two gates, no separate cell state


Two gates

Update gate \mathbf{z}_t — how much of the new candidate \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t to write in; (1 - \mathbf{z}_t) keeps the old state.
Reset gate \mathbf{r}_t — how much of the previous hidden state to use when computing the candidate.

\mathbf{z}_t = \sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_z [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t]\right) \mathbf{r}_t = \sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_r [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t]\right) \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t = \tanh\!\left(\mathbf{W}_h [\mathbf{r}_t \odot \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t]\right) \mathbf{h}_t = (1 - \mathbf{z}_t) \odot \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{z}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t


Pros: roughly 25% fewer parameters than an LSTM. Faster to train. Comparable performance on most tasks.
Cons: slightly less expressive for very long sequences. Hard to tell apart from LSTMs in benchmarks.








Precise gating doesn’t matter


LSTM and GRU achieve similar performance with different gate structures. What really matters is having some additive path for gradients to flow through long sequences.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
What the cells learn
Karpathy, The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks (2015)
Karpathy:

Trained character-level LSTMs on prose and on source code
Plotted the value of individual cells as the model read.



One cell tracked whether the text was inside a quotation – one value between quote marks, another outside.
One cell tracked line length – resetting at each newline.
One cell tracked bracket depth in code.


Nobody specified these! Next-character prediction alone caused these features to emerge because they help.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
section: The hidden state is a learned summary
text:
The hidden state is a learned summary

The general point
\mathbf{h}_t is a distributed summary of what matters so far – learned from the prediction objective.

Nobody wrote a quote detector. The model built one because quotes change what comes next.
A few cells are readable. Most are not — the summary is spread across all of them at once.

At only 128 hidden units, you can plot every cell and hunt for the readable ones (as Karpathy did).

At millions of units, however, single-cell inspection stops working

Understanding what a model represents becomes a research field of its own
Called interpretability or “explainable AI” (xAI)
This problem returns with transformers

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Why RNNs lost


The constraint
To compute \mathbf{h}_t, you need \mathbf{h}_{t-1}.

No parallelism over time.
Training a length-T sequence takes time proportional to T.
GPUs love parallelism


Transformers
Process every token in parallel during training.

Massive throughput
Scale to billions trillions of tokens
Same architecture at every size

Vaswani et al. (2017) — “Attention is all you need”.


The transformer paper is short and readable, so I’d recommend reading it

We’ll go through Figure 1 line-by-line on Monday morning

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Encoder–decoder seq2seq — the pre-transformer winner
seq2seq = sequence-to-sequence: the architecture that powered machine translation 2014–2017


Encoder
Reads the input sentence with an RNN. The final hidden state \mathbf{h}_T becomes a single fixed-size summary.

Decoder
A second RNN, initialised from \mathbf{h}_T. Generates the output one token at a time.


The bottleneck. All information about the input has to squeeze through one vector \mathbf{h}_T. For long sentences this breaks down — as the next slide makes concrete.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
A foreshadow of attention
The seq2seq bottleneck, in one example
Translating a 30-word sentence with vanilla seq2seq:


Encoder reads all 30 words → final hidden state \mathbf{h}_{30}.
Decoder starts from \mathbf{h}_{30}.
By the time the decoder is on word 5, it has forgotten the start of the input.

The information from “the cat” at the beginning has to travel through 30 RNN updates and then 5 decoder updates

The same problem: 35 multiplications by partial derivative matrices with magnitude < 1








Tip


Bahdanau et al. (2014) fixed this by letting the decoder look back at all the encoder’s hidden states — a weighted average, with weights the model learns to set. They called it attention.
It worked so well that, by 2017, someone asked: do we even need the recurrent layers?

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Still in use
Despite losing the headline race, RNNs (especially LSTMs / GRUs) are still chosen for:



Streaming applications — real-time speech recognition, online time-series control.
Small-data settings — LSTMs need less training data than transformers.
Time-series forecasting — where the autoregressive structure is a feature.
Embedded systems — RNNs run on tiny chips.


Social-science examples

Forecasting conflict events as a sequence over time (Hegre et al., 2022).
Roll-call vote prediction — modelling votes within a legislative session.
Event-history models as DL — survival analysis with sequential covariates.
Sentiment over conversations — speaker-to-speaker.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
RNNs for survival analysis
A social-science application of seq2one RNNs


Standard survival analysis (Cox PH, Kaplan-Meier) assumes:

Proportional hazards.
Fixed covariates (or simple time-varying ones).
Linear-in-covariates risk.

Recurrent survival models relax all three:

The hidden state \mathbf{h}_t summarises the full event history up to time t.
Output is the hazard rate at each time step.
Non-linear interactions emerge from the network.



Applications:

Patient trajectories (re-admission, mortality).
Customer churn with rich behavioural sequences.
Time-to-conflict-onset in international relations.
Firm bankruptcy with quarterly financials.

A drop-in upgrade when you have rich sequences and enough data to make the network worth its complexity.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
A worked social-science example
Predicting protest events from a stream of news headlines



Input: a sequence of daily news headlines for a country.
Output: probability of a protest in each subsequent day.
The model needs memory of recent escalating language.
An LSTM (or GRU) is a sensible architecture.


Even with transformers available, an LSTM-based forecaster is often:

Easier to train on small national news corpora.
Easier to deploy in real time on rolling data.
Easier to interpret per-timestep contribution.









Choosing between architectures


Ask not “what is the biggest model?” but “what is the right model for the data I have?”

Transformers work best when you have lots of data and lots of compute.
RNNs often work better when you have less data and/or compute

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Applications beyond text
Where RNNs/LSTMs are still load-bearing


Speech

End-to-end speech recognition (CTC-based RNNs from ~2014).
Live captioning systems.
Many production ASR pipelines retain RNNs.

Music

MIDI generation, ad-hoc accompaniment.
OpenAI’s MuseNet had transformer + RNN components.


Time series

Forecasting (sales, demand, finance).
Anomaly detection (server logs, IoT sensors).
Often beats classical models like ARIMA on long series.

Bioinformatics

DNA / protein sequence modelling (pre-AlphaFold).
Variant-effect prediction.








Tip


The common thread: moderate sequence lengths, streaming data, modest compute requirements. These are conditions where transformers’ parallel training will buy little.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (2/4)
text:
Lessons RNNs taught us
Carry into the rest of the course


Parameter sharing across position (also true of CNNs, attention).
Hidden state as compressed running summary (returns in transformers’ KV cache).
The vanishing-gradient problem (returns in deep transformers — fixed with residuals + LayerNorm).
Gating as a way to control information flow (returns in transformer MoE, mixture-of-experts routing).
Encoder-decoder as a template (still the shape of translation, summarisation).

Even though recurrence is now “out of date”, its constituent parts remain very useful!

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Where are we?
After yesterday’s lecture

Four days writing autodifferentiation by hand. From today, you never have to again

(except maybe in an exam 😉 )

Question for today:
How do we build neural networks at scale – in PyTorch, on real data, with a working classifier?







Concepts in practise


Moving from “understanding the algorithm” to “building a useful model”.



After today, every remaining lecture uses PyTorch.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
section: Warm-up · three questions from last time
text:
Warm-up · three questions from last time
≈ 5 min · shout it out

From yesterday

One gradient-descent update. w = 1, \frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = 0.5, learning rate \lambda = 0.1. What is the new w?
What does a loss function measure — and which loss did we use for continuous outcomes?
What do you backpropagate?


Everything here is from yesterday’s lecture!

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Warm-up · answers


Step against the gradient, scaled by \lambda: 
w_{\text{new}} = w - \lambda \frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = 1 - 0.1 \times 0.5 = 1 - 0.05 = 0.95

How wrong the model’s predictions are on the data, as a single number — lower is better. For regression we used mean squared error.
Often “the loss” but more technically you backpropagate the gradient of the loss

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
What PyTorch gives us

PyTorch is the autodiff library you built — only:

Faster — runs on GPU.
More general — operates on arbitrary tensors, not just scalars.
Better engineered — handles edge cases, numerical stability, parallelism.

The mental model is identical to your Value library. Same forward pass. Same backward pass. Same parameters, gradients, and updates.







Note


The point of the last two days was to demystify what PyTorch does. Now we let it do that work for us — and we focus on design instead of bookkeeping.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Tensors — the building block
You have met tensors already in the labs:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])             # 1-D tensor (a "vector")
W = torch.randn(4, 3)                          # 2-D tensor (a "matrix"), random-init
y = x @ W.T                                    # matrix multiplication
print(y.shape)                                 # torch.Size([4])


Tensor properties

.shape — dimensions.
.dtype — float32, int64, etc.
.device — cpu or cuda:0.
.requires_grad — should we track gradients?


Operations

@ or torch.matmul — matrix multiply.
+, -, *, / — element-wise.
torch.exp, torch.log — element-wise math.
.sum(), .mean() — reductions.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Autograd — backpropagation, automatically
x = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)
y = x ** 3 + 4 * x                  # y is a Value-like node — PyTorch builds the graph
y.backward()                        # backpropagate from y
print(x.grad)                       # → 16.0   (which is 3x² + 4 evaluated at x=2)

That is the whole API for autodiff in PyTorch.

You can build any expression with tensors, it will automatically track the resulting graph.
When you call .backward() on the scalar output tensor, you can then read off .grad from the inputs to see the results!
This is exactly the algorithm you have been working on by hand.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
section: The same model, the quick way — nn.Sequential
text:
The same model, the quick way — nn.Sequential
When the network is just a straight stack of layers, you don’t need to write a class at all. nn.Sequential chains modules and runs them in order:
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(3, 16),   # 3 inputs → 16 hidden
    nn.ReLU(),          # activation — now an explicit layer, not a function call
    nn.Linear(16, 1),   # 16 hidden → 1 output (logit)
)

This is exactly the TurnoutModel from the previous slide — same layers, same forward pass, same parameters:

\underbrace{3 \times 16 + 16}_{\text{layer 1} = 64} \;+\; \underbrace{16 \times 1 + 1}_{\text{layer 2} = 17} \;=\; \mathbf{81 \text{ parameters}}

The differences are cosmetic

torch.relu(...) (a function) becomes nn.ReLU() (a layer object)
There is no forward() to write as Sequential calls each module in order.

Use nn.Module when the forward pass branches or reuses and nn.Sequential for simple, feedforward stacks.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
section: A complete training script in 20 lines
text:
A complete training script in 20 lines
model     = TurnoutModel()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn   = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()

for epoch in range(50):
    for x_batch, y_batch in train_loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        y_logits = model(x_batch)                       # (B, 1) — a column
        loss = loss_fn(y_logits.squeeze(-1), y_batch)   # y_batch is (B,) — a row
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
    print(f"Epoch {epoch:02d}: train loss = {loss.item():.3f}")

Every PyTorch training loop in the world looks roughly like this.
We’ll change what’s inside the loop but the shape of this training protocol stays the same.







Why .squeeze(-1)? The last layer is 16 \to 1, so a batch of 32 comes out as shape (32, 1). The labels arrive as (32,) — i.e. a flat vector.

This is annoying, but we need to “squeeze” the output so it is also (32,).

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
The same pattern


Define a model (a Module whose forward() you wrote).
Pick a loss function (cross-entropy, MSE, …).
Pick an optimiser (Adam, SGD, …).
For each batch in your training data:

Zero the gradients.
Forward pass.
Compute the loss.
Backward pass.
One optimiser step.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
section: Activation functions — what they actually do
text:
Activation functions — what they actually do
A quick reminder why we need non-linearities
Without non-linearities, stacking layers buys us nothing: 
\mathbf{x} \mathbf{W}^{(1)\mathsf T} \mathbf{W}^{(2)\mathsf T} \cdots \mathbf{W}^{(L)\mathsf T} = \mathbf{x} \mathbf{W}^*\mathsf{T}

— still just a linear function of \mathbf{x}, regardless of L.
Non-linear activations between layers are what gives deep learning its advantage

They let the model bend, kink, and curve, not just separate with a single hyperplane.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
ReLU — the modern default



\sigma_{\text{ReLU}}(x) = \max(0, x), \qquad \sigma'_{\text{ReLU}}(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & x > 0 \\ 0 & x < 0 \end{cases}


Cheap.
No vanishing gradient on the positive side.
Sparse activations — many nodes output exactly 0.

The downside
Dead ReLUs. If a neuron’s pre-activation stays \leq 0, its gradient is always 0 — it stops learning.
Smoother variants (Leaky ReLU, GELU, SiLU) address this.


Default choice in 2026: use ReLU (or close cousin GELU) in hidden layers.
The overwhelming majority of feed-forward networks built in research do this. PyTorch: nn.ReLU().

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
section: ReLU vs GELU — the same kink, smoothed
text:
ReLU vs GELU — the same kink, smoothed

\sigma_{\text{ReLU}}(x) = \max(0, x)
\qquad\qquad
\sigma_{\text{GELU}}(x) = x \cdot \Phi(x)

\Phi is the standard-normal cumulative distribution function. GELU is just a softer version of ReLU.










Since backprop multiplies by \sigma', ReLU' is a step – exactly 0 for every negative input. GELU' is never exactly 0: at x = -1 it is -0.083.
Never really worth using GELU on a simple network, but very useful for transformers as we’ll see later!

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Sigmoid and tanh


Sigmoid
 \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}, \quad \sigma'(x) = \sigma(x)(1 - \sigma(x)) 

Squashes to (0, 1) — natural for binary probabilities.
Used at output of binary classifiers.
In hidden layers: vanishing gradients (flat tails).


Tanh
 \tanh(x), \quad \tanh'(x) = 1 - \tanh^2(x) 

Squashes to (-1, 1) — zero-centred.
Better than sigmoid for hidden layers, but still saturates.
Used in RNNs (Day 9!) and a few specialised places.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Identity, softmax — the output choices


Identity
\sigma(x) = x

For regression outputs — when y lives on the whole real line.
Never in hidden layers (except specialised cases).


Softmax
 \sigma_i(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} 

Squashes a vector of k scores into a probability distribution over k classes.
Used at output of multi-class classifiers.
Tied to cross-entropy loss.



Worked: softmax of \mathbf{z} = [2, 1, 0]
Exponentiate each score, then divide by their sum:

e^2 = 7.39, \quad e^1 = 2.72, \quad e^0 = 1.00, \quad \textstyle\sum = 11.11


\sigma(\mathbf{z}) = \left[\tfrac{7.39}{11.11},\ \tfrac{2.72}{11.11},\ \tfrac{1.00}{11.11}\right] = [0.67,\ 0.24,\ 0.09]

Three positive numbers that sum to 1, i.e. a probability over three classes

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
section: A worked social-science example — civil-war forecasting
text:
A worked social-science example — civil-war forecasting


Hegre et al. (2022) — Forecasting fatalities.

Predict country-month battle-deaths from a rich set of features.
A challenging benchmark in conflict studies.
The reference model is a deep feed-forward network.

The input vector: country indicators, lagged casualties, conflict history, geographic features, economic indicators.
The output: a single number — the predicted log fatalities for the next month.


A reasonable architecture:

Input: ~30 features.
Hidden 1: 128 → ReLU → dropout 0.2.
Hidden 2: 64 → ReLU → dropout 0.2.
Output: 1 (identity).

Train with MSE loss and Adam at \lambda = 10^{-3} for ~100 epochs.
This is exactly the kind of model you’ll build in today’s lab.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Plenary · predict the activations
≈ 10 min · in pairs

The pre-activation value:
z = -3.5
For each activation, compute (or estimate) the post-activation value \sigma(z):

Identity — \sigma(z) = z
ReLU — \sigma(z) = \max(0, z)
Sigmoid — \sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})
tanh — \sigma(z) = (e^{2z} - 1)/(e^{2z} + 1)

Then for each, give the derivative at z = -3.5.

Why does it matter that ReLU gives a 0 derivative and identity gives a derivative of exactly 1, while sigmoid/tanh give tiny derivatives?

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Plenary · answers




Activation

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Initialisation — why “all zeros” fails

Predict Suppose we set every weight to exactly 0 before training. What goes wrong on the first step — and could training ever recover?



Answer — the symmetry trap
If every weight starts at 0:

Every node in a layer gets the same input × same weights → the same output.
Every node gets the same gradient, so every node updates identically.
The network is effectively one node wide — symmetry never breaks, no matter how long you train.

Random initialisation breaks the symmetry. But the scale matters too: too big and activations explode; too small and they vanish — the same vanishing/exploding problem we saw with sigmoid, now driven by the weights, not the activation.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Xavier and He initialisation


Xavier (Glorot)
For sigmoid / tanh:  W^{(l)} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(0, \tfrac{2}{n^{(l-1)} + n^{(l)}}\right) 
Keeps the variance of activations stable across layers.
When the layer’s input and output dimensions are similar this reduces to the “fan-in” (LeCun) form \tfrac{1}{n^{(l-1)}}.

He (Kaiming)
For ReLU:  W^{(l)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tfrac{2}{n^{(l-1)}}) 
The factor of 2 compensates for the half of the distribution ReLU zeroes out.







You won’t usually set this by hand.


PyTorch’s nn.Linear defaults to a Kaiming-uniform variant. You should know this is happening but only override it if you have a reason.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Optimisers — what we’ll actually use



SGD — vanilla. Rarely best in practice.
SGD with momentum — better, still simple.
Adam — adaptive learning rates per parameter. Default first try.
AdamW — Adam with corrected weight decay. Default for transformers.


Learning rate

Most important hyperparameter you’ll set.
Reasonable starting points:

Adam: \lambda = 10^{-3}
SGD: \lambda = 10^{-2}

Too high → loss explodes.
Too low → loss crawls.








Modern practice


Use Adam with \lambda = 10^{-3}, then tune as needed.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Monitoring training

import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

model     = MyModel()                                    # nn.Module
loss_fn   = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

train_loader = DataLoader(train_set, batch_size=64, shuffle=True)
val_loader   = DataLoader(val_set,   batch_size=64)

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    model.train()
    for x_batch, y_batch in train_loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        y_pred = model(x_batch)
        loss   = loss_fn(y_pred, y_batch)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        val_loss = sum(loss_fn(model(x), y) for x, y in val_loader) / len(val_loader)
    print(f"Epoch {epoch:02d}: train={loss.item():.3f} val={val_loss.item():.3f}")

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
What’s new in this version


model.train() / model.eval() — toggles dropout and batch-norm behaviour (we’ll see why in Part 3).
torch.no_grad() — disables gradient tracking during evaluation (saves memory and time).
Validation loss — computed every epoch on held-out data.








Never compute training and validation loss without toggling train/eval


During training, several neural network features will operate differently than during testing (we’ll introduce some of these soon).

For each change, predict what happens to (a) training loss and (b) validation loss, then justify:


You increase the learning rate from 10^{-3} to 10^{-1}.
You add a third hidden layer (200 nodes wide).

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Activity · answers


Higher LR. Training loss might explode — overshoots minima. If it doesn’t explode, it may converge faster but more noisily. Validation loss tends to mirror.
Deeper model. Train loss → lower (more capacity to fit training data). Val loss → uncertain depending on data and model specification (more on this later).
No activations. Both losses suffer dramatically. The model is now linear regression with extra parameters — same hypothesis class, more parameters to wiggle. Converges to the optimal linear fit.
Frozen first layer. With random init, the first layer is essentially a fixed random projection. Sometimes still works (“random kitchen sinks”), but typically losses both rise vs. the unfrozen model.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
What you need to know
Stop & check

Before we go on to understand when models break, make sure you’re happy with the following:

Why does initialising every weight to zero stop the network from learning?
What does model.eval() change about dropout and batch norm?
Which optimiser and learning rate are the sensible first try?


If any of these are still fuzzy, flag it now!

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Neural networks are fickle
Even with the right loss, the right optimiser, and the right init, training can:



Diverge — loss explodes to infinity.
Stall — loss stops decreasing too early.
Overfit — train loss → 0, validation loss climbs.
Underfit — neither loss falls usefully.








Warning


You will encounter all of these in the labs this week. The point of this section is to give you the vocabulary to diagnose what’s happening — not to fix everything in one go.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Problem 1 — overfitting


Neural networks have many parameters. They can memorise the training set if you let them.

Training loss → 0.
Validation loss starts climbing.
The model has fit noise in the training data, not signal.







Tip


The diagnostic is the gap between training and validation loss curves — watch them every epoch.




Defences

Hold out a validation set.
Early stopping — stop when val loss bottoms out.
Dropout — random masking.
Weight decay — penalise large weights.
More data — when available.
Smaller model — when you can’t get more data.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Dropout
During training, with probability p, zero out each node’s output:




Forces the network to learn redundant representations.
Acts like an implicit ensemble of thinned sub-networks.
Standard: p = 0.2–0.5 on hidden layers; never on the output.
In PyTorch: nn.Dropout(p=0.2) after an (activated) layer.

Dropout is turned off at inference

model.eval() scales the learned weights as a result

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Problem 2 — vanishing gradients


For sigmoid / tanh:

Their derivatives are nearly zero for large |z|.
Backprop multiplies many derivatives via the chain rule.
In a deep network this product results in shrinking gradients.
Gradients near the input layer effectively vanish.
Early layers stop learning.








Fixes

Use ReLU-family activations (no flat tail for z > 0).
Normalise activations across the network → next slide.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Batch normalisation — the idea (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015)
Every layer learns against a moving target: as the layers before it update, the distribution arriving at this one shifts.

The fix After a layer’s pre-activation, rescale each feature so that — across the examples in the mini-batch — it has mean 0 and variance 1.


\text{BN}(z) = \gamma \cdot \underbrace{\frac{z - \mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_B^2 + \epsilon}}}_{\text{standardise}} + \beta

\mu_B, \sigma_B^2 — mean and variance of this one feature, over the examples in the batch. \gamma, \beta are learnable scale and shift parameters, one pair per feature.

Stop & check A batch of 32 examples enters a hidden layer of width 64. How many means \mu_B does batch norm compute?



Answer 64 — one per feature, each averaged over the 32 examples. The batch is the dimension we average away.

Because \gamma, \beta are learned, the network can undo the standardisation if the original scale was useful!


Why it helps
Stabilises activations across layers, stops distributions drifting during training, makes initialisation less critical, lets you use a larger learning rate.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Batch vs layer norm







Batch norm one \mu per feature, averaged down the batch. Needs a decent batch size. Predominantly used in CNNs.

Layer norm one \mu per example, averaged across its features. Batch-size independent — which is exactly why transformers use it (Day 10).

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
section: Diagnosing a run from its loss curves
text:
Diagnosing a run from its loss curves
≈ 3 min · in pairs













Match each panel to a diagnosis
Four training runs. Same model, same data — four different outcomes:

learning rate too high
overfitting
underfitting
healthy

Which is which — and what in the curves told you?

These are the curves you plot in today’s lab.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Diagnosing a run · answers


A — overfitting. Training keeps falling; validation bottoms out, then climbs. Fix: dropout or weight decay, early stopping, or more data — the defences from the overfitting slide.
B — healthy. Both curves fall together and the gap stays small. Fix: none. Leave it alone.
C — learning rate too high. The loss jumps around and drifts upwards. Fix: lower the learning rate — from 10^{-1} back towards 10^{-3}.
D — underfitting. Both curves flat and high from the first epoch. Fix: a bigger model, or train for longer.








Always inspect your loss curves!


When a run misbehaves, plot these two curves before touching anything else. The shape tells you which problem you have — and each problem has a different fix.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
section: A practical checklist for week 2 onwards
text:
A practical checklist for week 2 onwards


Always

Normalise input features.
Split: train / val / test, never peek at test.
Track training and validation loss per epoch.
Save model checkpoints.
Set and log random seeds.


Most of the time

Adam, \lambda = 10^{-3} as a starting point.
ReLU + He init for hidden layers.
Dropout 0.2 in fully-connected layers.
Batch norm between layers (CNNs); layer norm (sequences).
Increase model size gradually.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
section: What the textbooks don’t tell you…
text:
What the textbooks don’t tell you…

Everything so far has been about what to build.

But of course, as humans, we are prone to error
Programmers are no different

The worst kind of error is one you don’t spot:

The code runs
No exception is reported
Maybe the model even has slightly declining loss


We have to figure out what is intrinsically hard, from what we have ourselves made hard through our mistakes!

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
section: How to read a PyTorch error
text:
How to read a PyTorch error
The most common error you will see, and it tells you more than it looks:
model = nn.Linear(3, 16)      # expects 3 features
x = torch.randn(32, 10)       # but we hand it 10
model(x)

PyTorch stops with
RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (32x10 and 3x16)


Decoding it

mat1 is your data: 32 rows (the batch), 10 features.
mat2 is the layer’s weight matrix: 3 in, 16 out.
Matrix multiplication needs the inner numbers to match. 10 \neq 3.

So: the layer wanted 3 features per example and you gave it 10. Fix the layer, or fix the data — but the message has already told you which two numbers disagree.







When a shape error appears, print(x.shape) on the line above.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Incorrect broadcasting
Remember .squeeze(-1) from the training script? Here is what it was protecting you from.
y_pred = model(x_batch)        # shape (32, 1) — a column
y_true = y_batch               # shape (32,)   — a flat vector
loss = nn.MSELoss()(y_pred, y_true)

Predict PyTorch broadcasts these two shapes rather than complaining. What shape does the subtraction inside MSE produce — and how many numbers does the mean get averaged over?



Answer — (32, 32), and 1,024 numbers
Broadcasting pads the shorter shape on the left: (32,) becomes (1, 32). Then (32, 1) against (1, 32) stretches both into (32, 32).
This will compare every prediction against every label — all 1,024 pairs — and averaged the them. But only the 32 numbers on the diagonal were ever meaningful.
The loss still comes out as a plausible-looking number

It falls during training…
But the model learns nothing useful.









MSE does print a UserWarning (target size that is different to the input size). Read your warnings.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Forgetting zero_grad()
PyTorch accumulates gradients — every .backward() adds to .grad rather than replacing it.



Two batches, one weight, \lambda = 0.1
Batch 1 gives \frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = 0.5; batch 2 gives 0.3.
With zero_grad() — the second step uses 0.3: w \leftarrow w - 0.1 \times 0.3 = w - 0.03
Without it — .grad still holds batch 1’s number: w \leftarrow w - 0.1 \times \underbrace{(0.5 + 0.3)}_{0.8} = w - 0.08


Batch 1’s gradient is still steering the model several batches later.

Unlike momentum, the gradient grows without limit
The loss curve looks like a learning rate set far too high.







Why doesn’t PyTorch just do it for you?
Because accumulation is sometimes what you want! E.g. running four small batches and stepping once simulates a batch four times the size on a GPU that can’t hold one

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Consuming all your memory


The bug
losses = []
for x, y in train_loader:
    loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
    ...
    losses.append(loss)      # a tensor
loss is a node in the graph. Keeping it keeps every activation that produced it — for every batch of the epoch. Memory climbs until the run dies (you might see a segfault error)

The fix
losses = []
for x, y in train_loader:
    loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
    ...
    losses.append(loss.item())   # a float
.item() pulls a one-element tensor out as a plain Python number and drops the graph with it.


Two related tools worth knowing:

.detach() — same tensor, cut loose from the graph. Use when you want the values but not the history.
torch.no_grad() — a block where no graph is built at all. Use for validation and inference.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Having data on different devices

The error you will meet the first time you use a GPU
RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device, but found at least two devices, cuda:0 and cpu!


The rule The model and the data it is fed must sit on the same device. Move the model once, outside the loop. Move each batch as it arrives.
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model.to(device)                                  # once

for x, y in train_loader:
    x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)             # every batch







An annoying asymmetry that catches everyone


model.to(device) moves the model in place. x.to(device) does not — it returns a new tensor and leaves the original alone. So model.to(device) on its own works, and x.to(device) on its own silently does nothing. Tensors need the assignment: x = x.to(device).

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Always “smoketest” your training
The best debugging trick in deep learning, and it takes thirty seconds

Before training on the full dataset, take eight examples and train on those same eight, over and over:
x, y = next(iter(train_loader))
x, y = x[:8], y[:8]

for step in range(200):
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    if step % 50 == 0:
        print(step, loss.item())



Loss goes to almost zero
Your forward pass, loss, and optimiser all work. Any remaining problem is about generalisation.

Loss stays flat
You have a bug, not a hyperparameter problem. Eight examples is enough capacity for any network to memorise/overfit.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
section: Seeds — what they buy, and what they don’t
text:
Seeds — what they buy, and what they don’t
import torch, numpy as np, random
SEED = 324
torch.manual_seed(SEED); np.random.seed(SEED); random.seed(SEED)


What you get

The same weight initialisation.
The same shuffling and dropout masks.
The same numbers when you re-run on the same machine, same versions.


What you don’t

Reproducibility across different hardware, or a different PyTorch version.
Determinism on GPU by default — some CUDA kernels sum in a non-fixed order.
Anything at all if you seed after building the model.








Set the seed as the first thing in the script, and log it alongside the results.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Saving a model

Save the weights, not the object
torch.save(model.state_dict(), "model.pt")            # save

model = TurnoutModel()                                # rebuild the architecture
model.load_state_dict(torch.load("model.pt"))         # load the weights
model.eval()                                          # inference mode

A state_dict is a dictionary of tensors, one per parameter. torch.save(model, ...) also works — it pickles the whole object, including the path to your class, so it breaks the moment you rename a file or move a class. Save the dictionary.






Checkpoint every epoch where validation loss improves. That is early stopping, implemented: keep training, but keep the best weights you have seen.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Activity · find the bugs
≈ 8 min · in pairs
This loop runs without error. It also trains badly, and eventually crashes the machine. Find three problems.
model     = TurnoutModel()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn   = nn.MSELoss()
history   = []

for epoch in range(100):
    for x, y in train_loader:
        y_pred = model(x)
        loss   = loss_fn(y_pred, y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        history.append(loss)

    val = sum(loss_fn(model(x), y) for x, y in val_loader) / len(val_loader)
    print(f"epoch {epoch}: val = {val:.3f}")

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Activity · answers


No optimizer.zero_grad() before loss.backward(). Gradients accumulate across every batch of every epoch, so each step is driven by a growing sum of stale gradients.
history.append(loss) stores the tensor, not loss.item(). Every graph in the epoch is kept alive; memory climbs until the process is killed.
No model.train() / model.eval(), and no torch.no_grad() around validation. Dropout and batch norm stay in training mode while you evaluate, so the validation number is wrong — and building graphs you never backpropagate wastes memory and time.



A fourth, if you spotted it TurnoutModel outputs shape (B, 1) and the labels arrive as (B,). That is the broadcasting trap from earlier — it needs y_pred.squeeze(-1), and MSE will warn you about it exactly once per run.

title: Feed-forward networks in PyTorch
text:
Take stock
Where you are at the end of Day 5

You can:

Write a working feed-forward network in PyTorch.
Pick a sensible loss, optimiser, and learning rate.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
section: Warm-up · three questions from last time
text:
Warm-up · three questions from last time
≈ 5 min · shout it out


What forces an autoencoder to learn a compressed representation rather than copying its input?
What can you do with a trained VAE that you cannot do with a plain autoencoder — and which part of the loss makes it possible?
In the reparameterisation trick we write \mathbf{z} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \boldsymbol{\sigma} \odot \boldsymbol{\epsilon}. Why not just sample \mathbf{z} directly?

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
text:
Warm-up · answers


The bottleneck. The latent dimension is smaller than the input, so the network cannot pass the input through unchanged – it has to compress.
Sample new images from the latent space. The KL term in the VAE loss keeps the latent space organised around the origin, so a point drawn from \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}) decodes to something sensible. A plain autoencoder has no such guarantee – most latent points decode to nonsense.
Gradients cannot flow through a random sampling step. Writing \mathbf{z} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \boldsymbol{\sigma} \odot \boldsymbol{\epsilon} moves the randomness into \boldsymbol{\epsilon}, which has no parameters. The path from the loss back to \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{\sigma} is now deterministic, so backprop works.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
section: How do we feed text to a neural network?
text:
How do we feed text to a neural network?
A neural network takes numbers. Text is a sequence of characters / words / morphemes / utf-8 codepoints.

Tokenisation = the choice of what counts as one unit. The rest of the model — embeddings, attention, output layer — works on top of that decision.

Three granularities to choose from


Character

Tiny vocab (\sim 100)
Long sequences
Where we’re going to start


Word

Huge vocab (10^5+)
Out-of-vocabulary is a hard problem
What 1990s NLP used


Subword (BPE)

In-between (~50-100k)
Composable
What GPT, Claude, BERT use
(We’ll get to this on Day 11)

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
section: What does the text actually look like to the model?
text:
What does the text actually look like to the model?
The string "hello" is, to your computer, a sequence of bytes: [104, 101, 108, 108, 111].
To a language model, after tokenisation, it’s a sequence of token ids — typically much shorter:


As characters (tokens = chars)
"hello world" → [7, 4, 11, 11, 14, 0, 22, 14, 17, 11, 3] (ids illustrative)
11 tokens needed for the string

Each id picks one row from a small lookup table.


As BPE (tokens = subwords)
"hello world" → [15339, 1917]
Two tokens. Each picks one row from a vocab of ~100,000.
(These are the actual ids GPT-4’s tokeniser, cl100k, assigns — and its vocab is ~100k.)







Note


The choice of tokeniser determines the cost (sequence length) and the unit the model learns to work with. We’ll see both on Day 11.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
text:
A baby character tokeniser
Take all unique characters in some corpus. Number them 0, 1, 2, ….
text = "to be or not to be"
chars = sorted(set(text))      # [' ', 'b', 'e', 'n', 'o', 'r', 't']
stoi  = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(chars)}
itos  = {i: c for c, i in stoi.items()}

encode = lambda s: [stoi[c] for c in s]
decode = lambda ids: "".join(itos[i] for i in ids)

encode("to be") → [6, 4, 0, 1, 2].
Each integer is a token id.
The network will see and produce integers.







And that’s all we need!


Once each character/token has a unique integer id, we just need to figure out how to process sequences of them.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
section: We don’t want to one-hot encode
text:
We don’t want to one-hot encode
You might think to feed token id i as a one-hot vector \mathbf{e}_i \in \mathbb{R}^V:

For V = 50{,}000: every token becomes a 50,000-dim sparse vector (only one entry is a 1)
Massive but also orthogonal – the representation encodes no similarity at all.


Words have structure. “King” and “queen” should be close. “King” and “saucepan” should not. One-hot encodings know nothing about this.
We want a dense, learned, low-dimensional representation. That representation is called an embedding.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
section: An embedding is a lookup table
text:
An embedding is a lookup table

A mapping from token id i to a dense vector \mathbf{e}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d.
Implemented as a learnable embedding matrix \mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}.

Row i of \mathbf{E} is the embedding of token i.
Embedding lookup = “select row i”.
The entries of \mathbf{E} are just parameters — learned by backprop, like any other.


In PyTorch: nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=V, embedding_dim=d).

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
text:
Why embeddings end up meaningful
The distributional hypothesis (Harris, 1954):

Words that occur in similar contexts have similar meanings.



Train a model to predict words from their context.
The hidden representation must capture context-relevant similarity.
Words appearing in interchangeable contexts get nudged to similar embeddings.

Nobody defines “meaning” anywhere in this setup. Similar embeddings fall out of the prediction task on their own.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
text:
How embeddings actually get trained
Word2vec, in one slide


Skip-gram
Given a centre word, predict its neighbours (within a window).

Input: one word.
Output: a single softmax over the whole vocabulary (V slots), trained to put probability mass on each true neighbour.
Loss: cross-entropy.


CBOW (continuous bag-of-words)
Given the neighbours, predict the centre word.

The inverse problem.
Slightly more efficient to train.
Same family of result.



Why this works. To predict context, the model has to encode similarity-of-meaning into the embeddings — otherwise it can’t generalise across the millions of contexts in the training corpus.
GPT, Claude, and BERT all train embeddings the same way — as a side-effect of their primary task.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
text:
Can we afford that softmax?
The output layer, at real scale (Mikolov et al., 2013)
Our toy softmax had 5 slots. Google News word2vec has V = 3M.

The bill, per training pair
To normalise a softmax you must score every word: \mathbf{h}\,\mathbf{W}_{\text{out}} is 300 \times 3\text{M} = 900M multiplications — for one window, before one update. Multiply by billions of windows.


The fix — negative sampling
Swap “which of 3M words is the neighbour?” for a handful of yes/no questions:

The real pair from the corpus — (sat, cat) → target yes.
k fake pairs with randomly drawn words — (sat, quasar), (sat, invoice), … → target no.

Each question is a logistic regression on the two words’ vectors. With k = 5: one update touches 6 \times 300 = 1{,}800 output weights, not 900M — half a million times less work.

The embeddings come out about as good — and since we discard the output side anyway, nothing of value is lost.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
text:
The classic demonstration (Mikolov et al., 2013)
Word2vec embeddings, trained on a big corpus:

\mathbf{e}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{e}_{\text{man}} + \mathbf{e}_{\text{woman}} \ \approx \ \mathbf{e}_{\text{queen}}


Analogies become vector arithmetic. “King is to man as queen is to woman” — the relationship is encoded as a direction in the embedding space.
The model wasn’t trained to do analogies. It learned them as a by-product of predicting context words.







Warning


Real-world embeddings encode all statistical regularities of their training corpus — including the unsavoury ones. We come back to this.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
text:
Measuring “closeness” with cosine similarity
What does that \approx actually mean for two vectors?
We keep saying two embeddings are “close.” The standard measure is cosine similarity —- the cosine of the angle \theta between them:

\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert}


+1 → same direction (very similar).
0 → orthogonal (unrelated — exactly the one-hot case).
-1 → opposite direction.

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
text:
Calculating cosine similarity

A 2-D worked example
Let \mathbf{a} = (3, 4) and \mathbf{b} = (4, 3).

Dot product: \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = 3\times 4 + 4\times 3 = 24.
Lengths: \lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5 and \lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5.
So \cos\theta = \dfrac{24}{5\times 5} = \dfrac{24}{25} = 0.96 — nearly the same direction.

Now take \mathbf{c} = (4, -3): \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c} = 12 - 12 = 0, so \cos\theta = 0 — orthogonal, i.e. unrelated. (This is exactly what one-hot vectors are to each other.)


Try — 30 seconds in pairs Compute \cos\theta for \mathbf{a} = (1, 0) and \mathbf{b} = (1, 1).



Answer \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = 1\times 1 + 0\times 1 = 1; \lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert = 1 and \lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41.
\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{1\times 1.41} \approx 0.71 — a 45° angle. Halfway between “identical” and “unrelated.”

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
text:
The analogy, with actual numbers
Let’s earn that \approx in a toy 2-D embedding space
Suppose, in our tiny space, the embeddings are:

\mathbf{e}_{\text{king}} = (2, 1), \quad
\mathbf{e}_{\text{man}} = (1, 1), \quad
\mathbf{e}_{\text{woman}} = (1, 2)

Step 1 — do the arithmetic

\mathbf{e}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{e}_{\text{man}} + \mathbf{e}_{\text{woman}}
= (2 - 1 + 1,\; 1 - 1 + 2) = (2, 2)

Call this result \mathbf{r} = (2, 2), with length \lVert\mathbf{r}\rVert = \sqrt{2^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83.
Step 2 — find the nearest word by cosine similarity
We compare \mathbf{r} to three candidate embeddings (each of length 5, so every denominator is 2.83\times 5 \approx 14.14):

title: Building your own text-generating AI (1/4)
section: We can do the same thing with characters
text:
We can do the same thing with characters
Character-level embeddings work the same way:


Vocabulary V = 65 characters (uppercase + lowercase + punctuation + whitespace).
Embedding dim d = 32, for example
Embedding matrix: 65 \times 32 = 2{,}080 parameters. Next to nothing.

Each character gets a dense vector. Backprop tunes those vectors to be useful for the next-character prediction task.
